title: Asian Central Bank Rate Paths: A Comparative Analysis
abstract: A comparative look at how Asian central banks are navigating divergent inflation and growth pressures in 2026.
body:
## Divergent Paths in Asian Monetary Policy

As of April 2026, Asia's major central banks are charting increasingly divergent monetary policy paths, driven by uneven inflation dynamics, currency pressures, and domestic growth trajectories. The Bank of Japan (BoJ) remains the outlier, having ended its negative interest rate policy in 2024 and gradually raised its policy rate to 0.5% by early 2026. In contrast, the People's Bank of China (PBoC) has kept its one-year loan prime rate at 3.1% since late 2025, while the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has held its repo rate at 6.25% for three consecutive meetings. The Bank of Korea (BoK) and Bank of Thailand (BoT) have also paused, citing mixed signals from exports and household debt.

Analysts at Nomura note that this divergence reflects the region's varied exposure to global shocks. "Asia is not a monolith," said Sonal Varma, chief economist for India and Asia ex-Japan at Nomura, in a April 10, 2026 research note. "The BoJ is normalizing, China is easing, and others are stuck in neutral." The International Monetary Fund's April 2026 World Economic Outlook projects Asia's GDP growth at 4.2% for the year, down from 4.5% in 2025, with inflation averaging 2.8%.

## Bank of Japan: Cautious Normalization

The BoJ's journey toward policy normalization has been slow and deliberate. After ending yield curve control in 2024, the central bank raised its short-term policy rate to 0.25% in July 2024 and then to 0.5% in January 2026. Governor Kazuo Ueda has signaled that further hikes will depend on wage growth and inflation sustainability. Core inflation, excluding fresh food, stood at 2.1% in February 2026, above the BoJ's 2% target for the 23rd consecutive month. However, the yen's depreciation to 155 per dollar has complicated the outlook, as it raises import costs but boosts exporter profits.

"The BoJ is walking a tightrope," said Izumi Devalier, head of Japan economics at Bank of America Merrill Lynch, in a March 28, 2026 interview. "They want to normalize, but they can't afford to derail the fragile recovery." The BoJ's next policy meeting is scheduled for April 30, 2026, with markets pricing a 40% chance of a 25 basis point hike.

## China: Easing to Support Growth

In contrast, the PBoC has maintained an accommodative stance. The one-year loan prime rate (LPR) has been at 3.1% since October 2025, and the five-year LPR at 3.6%. The central bank has also used targeted liquidity injections and relaxed mortgage rules to support the property sector, which continues to weigh on growth. China's GDP expanded by 4.8% year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026, slightly below the government's target of around 5%. Consumer inflation remains subdued at 0.9% in March 2026, while producer prices have been in deflation for 18 months.

"The PBoC is prioritizing growth over inflation," said Ting Lu, chief China economist at Nomura, in an April 5, 2026 report. "With deflationary pressures persisting, further easing is likely, but the room is limited by the need to stabilize the yuan." The offshore yuan has weakened to 7.25 per dollar, near the lower end of the PBoC's tolerated range.

## India and South Korea: On Hold Amid Uncertainty

The RBI has kept its repo rate unchanged at 6.25% since August 2025, as it balances inflation and growth. Retail inflation eased to 4.3% in March 2026, within the RBI's target band of 2-6%, but food prices remain volatile. GDP growth for the fiscal year ending March 2026 came in at 6.7%, down from 7.2% the previous year. Governor Sanjay Malhotra has emphasized a data-dependent approach, with the next policy meeting on May 7, 2026.

"The RBI has little room to cut rates aggressively," said Aurodeep Nandi, India economist at Nomura, in a April 12, 2026 note. "Core inflation is sticky, and the fiscal deficit is wide." Similarly, the BoK has held its base rate at 3.0% since November 2025, as household debt remains high at 105% of GDP. South Korea's exports grew 3.2% year-on-year in March 2026, but the won's weakness against the dollar has added to imported inflation.

## Thailand and Indonesia: Balancing Act

The BoT has kept its policy rate at 2.0% since October 2025, as tourism recovery offsets weak exports. Inflation was 1.2% in March 2026, below the BoT's target range of 1-3%. However, the baht has depreciated by 4% against the dollar since January 2026, prompting the central bank to intervene sporadically. "The BoT is in a wait-and-see mode," said Euben Paracuelles, chief ASEAN economist at Nomura, in a March 30, 2026 interview. "They want to support growth but are wary of capital outflows."

Bank Indonesia (BI) has also paused, keeping its benchmark rate at 5.75% since December 2025. Inflation was 2.8% in March 2026, within BI's target of 2.5-4.5%. The rupiah has been relatively stable, but foreign reserves fell to $135 billion in March 2026 from $140 billion in December 2025. Governor Perry Warjiyo has stated that BI will maintain stability while supporting growth.

## Outlook: Data-Dependent and Fragile

Looking ahead, Asian central banks are expected to remain data-dependent, with policy moves hinging on inflation prints, currency movements, and global demand. The U.S. Federal Reserve's anticipated rate cuts in the second half of 2026 could provide some relief, but the timing remains uncertain. "The region's central banks are navigating a narrow path," said Nomura's Varma. "Any misstep could lead to capital flight or overheating." With global trade tensions simmering and China's recovery fragile, the divergence in Asian monetary policy is likely to persist through 2026.
